extracted.intended_audience: aspiring authors querying literary agents / writers seeking publication
extracted.subtask_description: Practical, experience-based advice for authors preparing and sending query letters and managing the agent-search process, with emphasis on persistence, interpreting responses, and revising manuscripts based on feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perseverance
rubrics_metrics.description: Be stubborn and refuse to ever give up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author advises not to give up until you've queried at least one hundred agents (or at minimum many more than a few dozen). Persistence is framed as essential to eventual success; initial rejections are expected and shouldn't prompt quitting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistent Work / Craft Improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Cultivate a constant desire to improve as a writer by putting words on paper and studying the craft.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write lots of words, study craft techniques, and read as much as possible. Ongoing labor—continual writing and learning—is presented as a necessary tool in the writer’s trunk for reaching publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teflon-Mentality (Handling Rejection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop a force field to deflect ego-smashing rejections so they bounce off and don’t stop your progress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect and accept rejection as part of the process. The piece warns that rejection continues even after getting an agent, so emotional resilience is necessary to 'plug away.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Patience with the Publishing Timeline
rubrics_metrics.description: Accept that the world of publishing runs on an alternate concept of time and get used to waiting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not expect quick responses from agents, editors, or publishers; cultivate patience and realistic expectations about turnaround times.

rubrics_metrics.name: Query Volume (how many agents to query)
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't think about giving up until you've queried at least one hundred agents (author says: 'Really').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While a tiny minority may land an agent from their first query, most writers need to query many agents. The numeric guidance is explicit: aim high in volume rather than stopping after a modest number like 40.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use manuscript requests as a signal of a solid query
rubrics_metrics.description: If you are getting requests for manuscripts, that tells me your query is solid—it's working.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Receiving requests is a positive milestone (a 'mile marker') indicating your query letter and pitch are effective. It suggests you should continue querying and focus on the manuscript itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret type of rejection to decide next steps
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish between form rejections and encouraging, specific rejections with feedback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form rejections could mean a detour—consult a developmental editor. Specific, encouraging rejections that point out problems may mean you should revise and resubmit, especially if multiple agents cite similar issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heed repeated feedback as a near-signal
rubrics_metrics.description: When more than one agent says the same thing needs to be fixed, that is a strong signal to revise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple agents giving the same critique indicates a substantive issue with the manuscript; prioritize those revisions. Detailed, lengthy feedback (e.g., 'feedback that takes up the entire page') is a strong sign you're close and should rejoice and act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revise and resubmit when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Do the revisions and massage that manuscript even more, if necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Act on substantive feedback—revise the manuscript thoroughly rather than abandoning it. Resubmitting after meaningful revision is positioned as part of the path to success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Look for qualitative 'road signs' that indicate you’re close
rubrics_metrics.description: Anecdotal signals—such as an agent reading to the end on a commute or telling a story about being unable to stop—indicate the manuscript grabbed attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personalized anecdotes from agents (e.g., finishing the book on the couch, reading on the train rather than stopping) are cues that your writing is compelling; these qualitative signs are meaningful progress indicators even if representation hasn’t been offered yet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Celebrate milestones but recognize they are steps
rubrics_metrics.description: When you receive an offer of representation, celebrate the milestone—it's a major achievement—but understand it's not the final stop.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take a moment to enjoy being offered representation, but remember there are further steps (e.g., getting a book deal). The author gives examples of small celebrations while noting 'so far' you’ve made it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek professional help when only form rejections arrive
rubrics_metrics.description: Form rejections could mean a detour: consult a developmental editor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If your submissions mostly receive impersonal form rejections, that may indicate deeper manuscript issues; professional editorial evaluation can identify structural or craft problems to address before further querying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use conferences and agent-approach techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Learn how to approach an agent at conferences (implied advice to prepare for face-to-face pitching).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece points readers toward learning conference-appropriate approaches as part of the broader querying strategy (e.g., linked guidance on approaching an agent).
